Q: Get the return type of a method based on fully qualified class name, method name, and method parameter types A:

The thing that trips people up here is that Scala's multiple parameter lists don't actually exist once you're down on the JVM — they're a compile-time convenience, nothing more. A method like

def multiParamGroups(a: String)(b: Int, c: Boolean): Double = 0.0

gets compiled into one flat method, same as if you'd written def multiParamGroups(a: String, b: Int, c: Boolean): Double. Compile the class and run javap -p on it and you can see it directly:

public java.lang.String noParamGroups();
public int zeroArgs();
public boolean multiArgs(java.lang.String, int);
public double multiParamGroups(java.lang.String, int, boolean);

Notice noParamGroups (no parens at all in the source) and zeroArgs() (an empty param list) come out as the exact same shape — a bare zero-arg method. So plain Java reflection actually covers every case in your question, as long as you flatten the parameter groups into one ordered list before calling getMethod:

def returnTypeOf(className: String, methodName: String, paramTypes: List[Class[_]]): Class[_] = {
  val clazz = Class.forName(className)
  clazz.getMethod(methodName, paramTypes: _*).getReturnType
}

returnTypeOf("invalid.so.MyClass", "noParamGroups", Nil)                                           // java.lang.String
returnTypeOf("invalid.so.MyClass", "zeroArgs", Nil)                                                 // int
returnTypeOf("invalid.so.MyClass", "multiArgs", List(classOf[String], classOf[Int]))                // boolean
returnTypeOf("invalid.so.MyClass", "multiParamGroups",
  List(classOf[String], classOf[Int], classOf[Boolean]))                                            // double

classOf[Int] and classOf[Boolean] resolve to the primitive int.class/boolean.class tokens in Scala, which lines up exactly with those erased signatures — no boxing headaches.

If you specifically want Scala reflection — which actually understands the grouped-parameter structure and gives you Int/Boolean/Double back instead of JVM-erased types — scala.reflect.runtime.universe does it:

import scala.reflect.runtime.{universe => ru}

val mirror = ru.runtimeMirror(getClass.getClassLoader)

def returnTypeOf(className: String, methodName: String, paramTypes: List[ru.Type]): ru.Type = {
  val classSymbol = mirror.staticClass(className)
  val overloads = classSymbol.toType.decl(ru.TermName(methodName)).asTerm.alternatives.map(_.asMethod)

  overloads.find { m =>
    val declared = m.paramLists.flatten.map(_.typeSignature)
    declared.length == paramTypes.length &&
      declared.zip(paramTypes).forall { case (d, p) => d =:= p }
  }.getOrElse(throw new NoSuchMethodException(methodName)).returnType
}

decl(...) grabs the symbol for that name; .asTerm.alternatives handles the overloaded case and just hands back a one-element list when there's no overloading. paramLists is a List[List[Symbol]] — one inner list per parameter group — so .flatten collapses multiParamGroups's two groups into [String, Int, Boolean] for comparison, and correctly collapses both noParamGroups (zero groups) and zeroArgs (one empty group) down to Nil. Comparing with =:= instead of == matters too — that's the real type-equality operator in Scala reflection, and plain == can give false negatives on types that are semantically identical but represented differently internally.

Run against your four methods:

returnTypeOf("invalid.so.MyClass", "noParamGroups", Nil)                                                 // String
returnTypeOf("invalid.so.MyClass", "zeroArgs", Nil)                                                       // Int
returnTypeOf("invalid.so.MyClass", "multiArgs", List(ru.typeOf[String], ru.typeOf[Int]))                  // Boolean
returnTypeOf("invalid.so.MyClass", "multiParamGroups",
  List(ru.typeOf[String], ru.typeOf[Int], ru.typeOf[Boolean]))                                            // Double

I compiled your exact class and ran both versions against it end to end — output matches String/Int/Boolean/Double for all four methods, no surprises.

Two caveats worth keeping in mind: decl only sees members declared directly on the class, so swap in member if the method could be inherited from a trait or superclass. And this is specifically Scala 2's reflection API — Scala 3 moved to a different TASTy-based model, so if MyClass were compiled with Scala 3 you'd want its equivalent, or just fall back to the Java reflection version above, which doesn't care what compiler produced the bytecode.

Q: How can I make my axes visible with matplotlib? A:

TL;DR: The axes lines in Matplotlib are called spines. In your code, you are setting plt.rcParams['axes.edgecolor']='k', but you are doing it after you've already created the figure and axes. rcParams only apply to plots generated after the setting is changed.

Additionally, Jupyter Notebooks (especially if you are using a dark theme) often default these spines to white or transparent. When you set ax.patch.set_visible(False), you make the background transparent, causing white spines to vanish completely against white backgrounds.

I think adding this might work:

for spine in ax.spines.values():
    spine.set_visible(True)
    spine.set_color('black')

If that doesn't work, add this at the top:

plt.rcParams['axes.edgecolor'] = 'black'

That's a global parameter.

Q: Failed loading /usr/local/IonCube/ioncube_loader_lin_5.3.so A:

The system you migrated from uses a different version of PHP and you are using the wrong configuration file.

load up phpinfo and look for "Loaded Configuration File"

update your settings to use the config file mentioned by phpinfo.

I had a related issue with cron jobs for magento which gave me the same errors.
In my case PHP 5.6 > PHP 7

All the files were present, but what a mentioned above showed me the root of the error.

OLD COMMAND +

/usr/local/bin/php -c /usr/local/lib/php.ini /home/devlivingfresh/public_html/bin/magento cron:run | grep -v "Ran jobs by schedule" >> /home/devlivingfresh/public_html/var/log/magento.cron.log

NEW COMMAND

/usr/local/bin/php -c /opt/cpanel/ea-php70/root/etc/php.ini /home/devlivingfresh/public_html/bin/magento cron:run | grep -v "Ran jobs by schedule" >> /home/devlivingfresh/public_html/var/log/magento.cron.log

Q: How to run jq from gitbash in Windows? A:

In my case, I have fixed it in Windows10 while practicing a scenario of "Techworld with Nana" course, as per the below steps:

  1. open "cmd" prompt (Run as administrator)

  2. curl -L -o /usr/bin/jq-win64.exe

    Download it here

  3. You can add C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin path to your environment variables. If you follow this step, ignore the below steps.

    [OR]

    Go to the directory where jq is downloaded: C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin and copy the file to C:\ drive

  4. Add the path C:\ to "path" environment variable. This PC → Properties → Advanced system settings → Environment Variables → Edit → New. Then add the path (where you copied jq.exe, i.e., C:\) and Save it.

  5. Now open a new "cmd" prompt, jq --version

Q: Purpose of the crossorigin attribute...? A:

The crossorigin attribute in HTML elements like <img>, <script>, <audio>, and <video> is used to configure the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) settings when fetching resources from a different origin.

Why is it needed?

By default, browsers send cross-origin requests for media or scripts without requesting CORS authorization. While the resource will still load, its usage within the browser becomes restricted due to security mechanisms (e.g., Same-Origin Policy):

  • For <script> tags: Errors occurring inside a cross-origin script will be masked as a generic "Script error." on window.onerror unless CORS is explicitly enabled using crossorigin.
  • For <img> tags: Loading a cross-origin image onto a Canvas element without crossorigin will mark the canvas as "tainted," preventing operations like toDataURL() or getImageData().

Attribute Values

The crossorigin attribute supports two primary keyword values:

  1. anonymous (or just crossorigin=""):

    • Sends a CORS request with an Origin header.
    • Does not include credentials (such as cookies, HTTP authentication, or TLS client certificates) in the request.
    • If the server responds with an appropriate Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, the resource can be safely accessed without browser restrictions.

  2. use-credentials:

    • Sends a CORS request that includes user credentials (cookies, authentication headers).
    • The server must explicitly respond with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true along with matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers for the request to succeed.

For a complete breakdown with detailed examples and edge cases, feel free to check out my detailed guide: HTML crossorigin Attribute – Specifying CORS Request Modes.
